questions.question: What would be the electron dot structure of carbon dioxide which has the formula CO₂?
answer_steps: Carbon (4 valence electrons) shares two pairs of electrons with each oxygen atom (6 valence electrons).
So there are two double bonds: O=C=O. Each atom then has eight electrons in its outer shell.

questions.question: What would be the electron dot structure of a molecule of sulphur which is made up of eight atoms of sulphur? (Hint: the eight atoms of sulphur are joined together in the form of a ring.)
answer_steps: Each sulphur atom (6 valence electrons) shares one pair with each of its two neighbours in the ring.
So S₈ is a ring of eight S atoms joined by single bonds; each S also keeps two lone pairs.

questions.question: How many structural isomers can you draw for pentane?
answer_steps: Three: n-pentane (straight chain), 2-methylbutane (isopentane) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane).
All have the formula C₅H₁₂ but different structures.

questions.question: What are the two properties of carbon which lead to the huge number of carbon compounds we see around us?
answer_steps: Catenation: carbon atoms can link with each other to form long chains, branches and rings.
Tetravalency: each carbon can bond with four other atoms of carbon or other elements.

questions.question: What will be the formula and electron dot structure of cyclopentane?
answer_steps: Formula: C₅H₁₀.
Five carbon atoms form a ring with single bonds; each carbon shares one pair with each neighbouring carbon and one pair with each of its two hydrogens.

questions.question:
Draw the structures for the following compounds.

(i) Ethanoic acid

(ii) Bromopentane

(iii) Butanone

(iv) Hexanal

Are structural isomers possible for bromopentane?
answer_steps: (i) CH₃–COOH (ii) CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–Br
(iii) CH₃–CO–CH₂–CH₃ (iv) CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CHO
Yes: the bromine atom can be on carbon 1, 2 or 3 (1-, 2- and 3-bromopentane), and the chain can also be branched.

questions.question:
How would you name the following compounds?

(i) CH₃–CH₂–Br

(ii) H–CHO (a carbon atom with one hydrogen, joined by a double bond to oxygen and a single bond to another hydrogen)

(iii) H–C≡C–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃
answer_steps: (i) Bromoethane
(ii) Methanal (formaldehyde)
(iii) Hexyne (hex-1-yne)

questions.question: Why is the conversion of ethanol to ethanoic acid an oxidation reaction?
answer_steps: Ethanol gains oxygen (and loses hydrogen) when it changes to ethanoic acid:
$\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + 2[O] \rightarrow CH_{3}COOH + H_{2}O}$

questions.question: A mixture of oxygen and ethyne is burnt for welding. Can you tell why a mixture of ethyne and air is not used?
answer_steps: With air, ethyne burns incompletely (air has only about 21% oxygen), giving a sooty flame that is not hot enough.
With pure oxygen it burns completely and gives a very hot flame (about 3000 °C) that can melt metals: $\mathrm{2C_{2}H_{2} + 5O_{2} \rightarrow 4CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$

questions.question: How would you distinguish experimentally between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid?
answer_steps: Add sodium hydrogencarbonate to each.
The carboxylic acid gives brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide (which turns lime water milky); the alcohol does not: $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}COONa + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}$

questions.question: What are oxidising agents?
answer_steps: Substances that can add oxygen to other substances (or remove hydrogen from them) are oxidising agents.
Examples: alkaline potassium permanganate and acidified potassium dichromate.

questions.question: Would you be able to check if water is hard by using a detergent?
answer_steps: No.
Detergents form lather and no scum even in hard water, so they cannot show whether water is hard. Soap is used for that test.

questions.question: People use a variety of methods to wash clothes. Usually after adding the soap, they 'beat' the clothes on a stone, or beat them with a paddle, scrub with a brush or the mixture is agitated in a washing machine. Why is agitation necessary to get clean clothes?
answer_steps: The oily dirt is trapped inside micelles, but it is stuck to the cloth.
Agitation pulls the dirt and micelles away from the cloth so they can be rinsed off with water.

questions.question: Ethane, with the molecular formula C₂H₆ has
questions.explanation: One C–C bond and six C–H bonds: 7.
option_feedback: Do not forget the C–C bond.
Correct!
There are six C–H bonds and one C–C bond.
Count again: 6 + 1 = 7.

questions.question: Butanone is a four-carbon compound with the functional group
questions.explanation: The suffix -one means a ketone group.
option_feedback: Acids end in -oic acid.
Aldehydes end in -al.
Correct!
Alcohols end in -ol.

questions.question: While cooking, if the bottom of the vessel is getting blackened on the outside, it means that
options: the food is not cooked completely.
the fuel is not burning completely.
questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion leaves unburnt carbon (soot), which blackens the vessel.
option_feedback: The blackening is on the outside: it is soot from the fuel.
Correct!
The cause is too little air, not wet fuel.
Complete burning gives a clean blue flame and no soot.

questions.question: Explain the nature of the covalent bond using the bond formation in CH₃Cl.
answer_steps: Carbon has 4 valence electrons, hydrogen 1 and chlorine 7.
Carbon shares one pair of electrons with each of the three hydrogen atoms and one pair with the chlorine atom: four single covalent bonds.
Each atom gets a stable arrangement (H: 2 electrons; C and Cl: 8). No electrons are transferred, so no ions form: the bonds are covalent.

questions.question:
Draw the electron dot structures for

(a) ethanoic acid.

(b) H₂S.

(c) propanone.

(d) F₂.
answer_steps: (a) Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH: the CH₃ carbon shares single pairs with three H and the second carbon; the second carbon shares a double bond (two pairs) with one O and a single pair with the O of the –OH group, which shares a pair with H.
(b) H₂S: sulphur shares one pair with each hydrogen and keeps two lone pairs.
(c) Propanone, CH₃COCH₃: the middle carbon shares a double bond with oxygen and single pairs with the two CH₃ carbons.
(d) F₂: the two fluorine atoms share one pair (a single bond); each keeps three lone pairs.
In every structure, each atom except hydrogen has eight electrons around it; hydrogen has two.

questions.question: What is an homologous series? Explain with an example.
answer_steps: A series of compounds with the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit.
Example: the alkanes CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈, C₄H₁₀; or the alcohols CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH.

questions.question: How can ethanol and ethanoic acid be differentiated on the basis of their physical and chemical properties?
answer_steps: Physical: ethanol has a pleasant smell and a melting point of 156 K; ethanoic acid smells like vinegar and freezes at 290 K. Ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red; ethanol does not.
Chemical: ethanoic acid gives carbon dioxide with sodium hydrogencarbonate: $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}COONa + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}$
Ethanol gives no gas with sodium hydrogencarbonate.

questions.question: Why does micelle formation take place when soap is added to water? Will a micelle be formed in other solvents such as ethanol also?
answer_steps: The long carbon tail of soap does not dissolve in water while the ionic head does; so the tails cluster inwards and the heads face the water, forming micelles.
No: the carbon tail also dissolves in ethanol, so micelles do not form.

questions.question: Why are carbon and its compounds used as fuels for most applications?
answer_steps: They burn in air giving a lot of heat and light.
Many of them burn with a clean flame, are easy to store and transport, and have a high calorific value.

questions.question: Explain the formation of scum when hard water is treated with soap.
answer_steps: Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts.
These react with soap to form insoluble calcium and magnesium salts of the fatty acids, a white precipitate called scum.

questions.question: What change will you observe if you test soap with litmus paper (red and blue)?
answer_steps: Soap solution is basic.
It turns red litmus blue and leaves blue litmus unchanged.

questions.question: What is hydrogenation? What is its industrial application?
answer_steps: The addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated compound in the presence of a nickel catalyst: $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + H_{2} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{6}}$
It is used to convert vegetable oils into vanaspati ghee (solid fat).

questions.question: Which of the following hydrocarbons undergo addition reactions: C₂H₆, C₃H₈, C₃H₆, C₂H₂ and CH₄.
answer_steps: C₃H₆ (propene) and C₂H₂ (ethyne).
They are unsaturated (double and triple bonds); the others are saturated alkanes.

questions.question: Give a test that can be used to differentiate between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
answer_steps: Burn them: saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame; unsaturated ones burn with a sooty yellow flame.
(Unsaturated hydrocarbons also decolourise bromine water, which saturated ones do not.)

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of the cleaning action of soaps.
answer_steps: A soap molecule has an ionic (hydrophilic) head and a long hydrocarbon (hydrophobic) tail.
In water, soap molecules form micelles: the tails dissolve in the oily dirt at the centre and the heads face the water.
The micelles stay suspended in water; rinsing and agitating wash away the dirt trapped in them.

questions.question:
**Assertion (A):** C₄H₈, C₄H₆ and C₄H₁₀ are members of the same homologous series.

**Reason (R):** C₄H₈, C₄H₆, C₃H₄, C₃H₆, C₂H₄, C₂H₂ are unsaturated hydrocarbons.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.explanation: A is false: they have the same number of carbons but different general formulas (alkene, alkyne, alkane), so they belong to different series. R is true.
option_feedback: Check the Assertion again: it is false, because they belong to three different series: alkene, alkyne and alkane.
Check the Assertion again: it is false, because they belong to three different series: alkene, alkyne and alkane.
Check the Assertion again: it is false, because they belong to three different series: alkene, alkyne and alkane.
Correct! A is false: they belong to three different series: alkene, alkyne and alkane. R is true: all six listed compounds have a double or triple bond.

questions.question:
A hydrocarbon with the formula CₓHᵧ undergoes complete combustion as shown in the following equation: $\mathrm{2C_{x}H_{y} + 9O_{2} \rightarrow 6CO_{2} + 6H_{2}O}$

(a) What are the values of 'x' and 'y'?

(b) Give the chemical (IUPAC) name of the hydrocarbon.

(c) Is CₓHᵧ a saturated or an unsaturated hydrocarbon? Describe its electron dot structure.

(d) Name the alcohol which on heating with conc. H₂SO₄ will produce the above hydrocarbon CₓHᵧ.

(e) Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction of CₓHᵧ with hydrogen gas in presence of nickel.
answer_steps: (b) Propene
(c) Unsaturated: CH₃–CH=CH₂ has one C=C double bond (two shared pairs) and single bonds to the hydrogens.
(d) Propanol (propan-1-ol): $\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}OH \rightarrow C_{3}H_{6} + H_{2}O}$
(e) $\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6} + H_{2} \rightarrow C_{3}H_{8}}$

questions.question: The earth's crust has only ____ % carbon in the form of minerals.
questions.explanation: The crust has only 0.02% carbon in minerals (and the air has 0.03% carbon dioxide).
option_feedback: Correct!
Much less: only 0.02%.
Much less: only 0.02%.

questions.question:
(a) Explain the esterification reaction with a chemical equation and write the uses of esters.

(b) Write the properties of ethanoic acid.
answer_steps: (a) A carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst to give a sweet-smelling ester: $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + CH_{3}CH_{2}OH \rightarrow CH_{3}COOCH_{2}CH_{3} + H_{2}O}$
Esters are used in perfumes and as flavouring agents; they are also used to make soap (saponification).
(b) Ethanoic acid is a colourless liquid with the smell of vinegar; it freezes at 290 K (glacial acetic acid), turns blue litmus red and gives carbon dioxide with carbonates.

questions.question:
(a) Differentiate between soap and detergent.

(b) Write the names and formulae of the functional groups in propanol and propanone.
answer_steps: (a) Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids and form scum in hard water; detergents are sulphonate or ammonium salts and work well in hard water.
(b) Propanol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH: alcohol group, –OH.
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃: ketone group, >C=O.

questions.question: The bond in a molecule of nitrogen, N₂, is a:

option_feedback: That is hydrogen, H₂.
Nitrogen atoms share electrons.

questions.explanation: Graphite has free electrons between its layers; diamond does not.
option_feedback: Graphite does conduct.
Correct!

Diamond does not conduct.

option_feedback: Correct!
That is propane, an alkane.
That is not an alcohol of this series.
That is the member before ethanol.

questions.question: Covalent compounds usually have low melting points because:

questions.question: What are structural isomers? Give the two isomers of butane.
answer_steps: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are structural isomers.
Butane, C₄H₁₀: n-butane (straight chain, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃) and isobutane (branched, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃).

questions.question: What is saponification? Write the equation.
answer_steps: The reaction of an ester with sodium hydroxide to give an alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid; it is used to make soap.
$\mathrm{CH_{3}COOC_{2}H_{5} + NaOH \rightarrow CH_{3}COONa + C_{2}H_{5}OH}$

questions.question: Write one balanced equation each for (i) combustion (ii) addition (iii) substitution reactions of carbon compounds, naming the condition needed.
answer_steps: (i) $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \rightarrow CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$ (in oxygen, giving heat and light)
(ii) $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4} + H_{2} \rightarrow C_{2}H_{6}}$ (nickel catalyst)
(iii) $\mathrm{CH_{4} + Cl_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}Cl + HCl}$ (in sunlight)

questions.question: Write the IUPAC names of: (i) CH₃COCH₃ (ii) CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (iii) CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl
answer_steps: (i) Propanone
(ii) Butanoic acid
(iii) Chloropropane

questions.question: Describe the reactions of ethanoic acid with (i) ethanol (ii) sodium hydroxide (iii) sodium carbonate (iv) sodium hydrogencarbonate. What is glacial acetic acid?
answer_steps: (i) $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + CH_{3}CH_{2}OH \rightarrow CH_{3}COOCH_{2}CH_{3} + H_{2}O}$ (acid catalyst; a sweet-smelling ester)
(ii) $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + NaOH \rightarrow CH_{3}COONa + H_{2}O}$
(iii) $\mathrm{2CH_{3}COOH + Na_{2}CO_{3} \rightarrow 2CH_{3}COONa + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}$
(iv) $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + NaHCO_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}COONa + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}$
Pure ethanoic acid freezes at 290 K and looks like ice in cold weather, so it is called glacial acetic acid.

questions.question: Explain why carbon forms a very large number of compounds. Describe saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons with one example each, and draw (describe) the structures of ethane and ethene.
answer_steps: Catenation: carbon atoms join each other into long chains, branches and rings.
Tetravalency: each carbon bonds with four atoms of carbon or other elements, with strong bonds.
Saturated hydrocarbons have only single C–C bonds, e.g. ethane, C₂H₆: H₃C–CH₃.
Unsaturated hydrocarbons have a double or triple bond, e.g. ethene, C₂H₄: H₂C=CH₂.
Saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean flame and give substitution reactions; unsaturated ones give a sooty flame and addition reactions.

questions.question:
A welder uses a mixture of ethyne and oxygen. At home, the bottom of Aarav's mother's cooking pot has turned black because the gas burner holes are blocked.

(i) Why is ethyne burnt with oxygen and not air for welding? (1)

(ii) What does the black bottom of the pot tell you about the burning? (1)

(iii) Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of methane (the main part of LPG/natural gas). OR Why is incomplete combustion dangerous? (2)
answer_steps: (i) Pure oxygen makes it burn completely, giving a very hot flame that melts metals.
(ii) The fuel is not burning completely; unburnt carbon (soot) is deposited.
(iii) $\mathrm{CH_{4} + 2O_{2} \rightarrow CO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}$ OR It produces carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas, and wastes fuel.

questions.question:
In a village, Riya's grandmother washes clothes with soap in well water, but the soap does not lather and a white solid floats on top. Riya brings a detergent powder and the clothes are washed easily.

(i) What is the white solid called? (1)

(ii) What makes the well water hard? (1)

(iii) Explain how soap removes oily dirt. OR Why does the detergent work in hard water? (2)
answer_steps: (i) Scum.
(ii) Calcium and magnesium salts dissolved in the water.

(iii) Soap molecules form micelles: the hydrocarbon tails hold the oily dirt in the centre and the ionic heads face the water, so the dirt is rinsed away. OR Detergents do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so no scum forms.
